what_it_does: Disaggregated memory is an architecture where memory is physically separated from the CPU and connected over a network (rather than the memory being plugged directly into the motherboard next to the processor), allowing memory to be pooled and shared across many servers. This is efficient for resource utilization but introduces network latency on every memory access. Pointer-chasing workloads — programs that navigate linked data structures like trees or linked lists, where each step tells you where the next step is — are especially hurt by this latency because each step depends on the result of the previous one, so you cannot prefetch or cache effectively. pulse moves the traversal computation itself to processing elements that live near or inside the memory nodes, so the chain of pointer hops happens without any data crossing the network until the final answer is ready. The system supports a range of linked data structures through a programmable traversal interface and can distribute work across multiple memory nodes for large datasets.
